text: Steep pavment entrance: Subject: Formal Request for Remedial Works to Pavement and Road Level at Driveway Entrance Dear Sir/Madam, I am writing to raise a concern regarding the sudden drop in level between the pavement and the street outside my property at 46 Dunblane Road, SE96RS, where the entrance to my driveway meets the road. I would also be grateful for written confirmation of any proposed action and the expected timescale for addressing this issue. Thank you for your time and consideration. text: Dangerous 2 storey high dead shrubs dangling off broken tree branch overhanging pavement: This report relates directly to the same matter as closed report 10230147, where the status was changed to 'not the council's responsibility'. Simply closing that report does not remove the immediate safety risk to the public. While the tree or shrub may originate on private land, this column of dead vegetation (around 5 meters high) has already snapped off a large branch and is dangling directly over a busy public pavement on Crossway near Pointer Close. Under Section 154 of the Highways Act 1980, the council has the statutory power and duty to serve an enforcement notice on private landowners to remove hazards overhanging the public highway, or to carry out emergency work to make it safe and recover the costs. Closing report 10230147 does not discharge the council's duties. Now that this severe hazard has been formally logged and brought to your attention, the council remains officially on notice. If someone is struck or injured by this falling debris, failing to exercise your highway safety enforcement powers leaves the council exposed regarding its duty to keep public footpaths safe. Over time, the condition of the infrastructure has deteriorated significantly. A number of the post foundations have shifted, causing the posts to become unstable, and several of the connecting chains have broken. As a result, the area has become both unsightly and a potential health and safety hazard. Loose metal chains are now present in places and there is a risk of injury to pedestrians, students, parents and other members of the public using the footway. Given the high volume of foot traffic outside the academy, we would be grateful if this matter could be assessed as a priority. We would appreciate a site inspection and advice on the timescale for repair or replacement of the damaged posts and chains. We believe that remedial works would not only improve safety but also enhance the appearance of the local streetscape. Please let me know if any further information or photographs would assist your assessment.

text: Underpass under A23 at The Dingle, Quantock Close, Crawley: Subject: URGENT FORMAL COMPLAINT - Dangerous Slippery Underpass - Child Injured - A23 Underpass at The Dingle / Quantock Close Date of Incident: 12th October 2026 at 15:19 Exact Location: The pedestrian underpass / subway under the A23 (Crawley Avenue) linking The Dingle / Quantock Close (RH11) to Ifield Community College, Crawley. Dear Sir / Madam, I am making a formal complaint regarding the dangerous condition of the above underpass. The Incident: On 12th October at 15:19, my young son fell face-first inside this underpass. He sustained bruising to his face and a swollen, painful eye. As you can see in the attached photo, the floor was wet with a thin layer of water that was highly reflective and extremely slippery. There was no visible large puddle, which makes it more dangerous as the hazard is not obvious. Thankfully there was no broken glass on the ground at that time, although broken glass is frequently present in this underpass. The Hazard - As shown in evidence: As the attached photo taken on the day shows, the surface appears to have a sheen and is slippery, with wet leaves. It is not a major flood, but a persistent thin film of water that does not drain. This creates a deceptive, ice-like surface. I nearly slipped myself the following day despite walking very carefully. This condition occurs every time it rains and becomes worse in winter with rain and snow. Residents have reported this before. Why this is urgent: This underpass is used daily by hundreds of children going to Ifield Community College, as well as parents, elderly residents, and commuters from Quantock Close and The Dingle. It is the main pedestrian route and it is not safe. I have attached: 1. Photo of the slippery, wet floor inside the underpass on 12/10/2026 2. Map showing the exact location of the underpass I formally request: 1. Immediate inspection and deep clean of the underpass. 2. Installation of anti-slip surfacing. 3. Repair of the drainage to prevent standing water. 4. Regular maintenance to remove litter, broken glass, and wet leaves, and a review of lighting and handrails. 5. Written confirmation of what action will be taken and within what timescale. Please treat this as a serious injury risk. If this hazard is not addressed and another child is injured, I will escalate this to my local councillor and the Health and Safety Executive. Please provide a reference number for this complaint. Yours faithfully,

text: Rat run road use excessive for small lanes traffic slowing measures needed: Location: Slipton Lane, Slipton, NN14 3AR, outside Lily House on the corner. text: Cressex Roac, approaching the roundabout on Marlow Road. Island position and safe crossing: Live near this junction and have repeatedly witnessed schoolchildren crossing the road at dangerous locations. I have also seen wheelchair users struggling to navigate the existing layout. Vehicles travel through the junction at considerable speed. The existing refuge islands do not appear to provide a clearly defined, continuous pedestrian crossing route, and there appear to be missing or inadequate dropped kerbs and flush transitions. There is no obvious safe and accessible crossing immediately adjacent to the location. This is particularly concerning given the nearby educational facilities, including Wycombe High School, John Hampden Grammar School, Mapledean Nursery School, Mapledean Family Hub and Chepping View Primary Academy. Children, young people and families use the surrounding roads, making this an important public safety concern. I request an urgent site inspection and formal highway safety and accessibility assessment. Please assess the crossing route, dropped kerbs, tactile paving, refuge islands, visibility, vehicle speeds and turning movements, pedestrian demand, and relevant collision or near-miss records. Please assess the location against applicable Department for Transport guidance, including Inclusive Mobility and Guidance on the Use of Tactile Paving Surfaces, relevant highway design standards, and the council’s duties under section 149 of the Equality Act 2010. I request appropriate permanent improvements, including accessible crossing points and, if justified by the assessment, a formal pedestrian crossing. Please also consider interim safety measures if an immediate risk is identified. This is not a hypothetical concern: I have personally witnessed children crossing dangerously and wheelchair users struggling at this location. Please treat this as an urgent highway safety issue and confirm the findings, proposed action and timescale for improvements. The council should not wait for a serious collision before addressing these concerns.

With the pavement already so narrow, the encroaching vegetation makes it increasingly difficult to maintain a safe distance from passing traffic. I am genuinely concerned that it is only a matter of time before someone is seriously injured along this stretch. I would ask the council to: * Arrange for the hedgerow and vegetation to be cut back sufficiently to restore the full usable width of the pavement. * Clear the accumulated vegetation and debris. * Inspect and repair the cracked and deteriorating pavement surface. * Consider whether additional pedestrian safety measures are necessary, given the 60 mph speed limit and the use of this route by families walking to and from school. We are constantly encouraged to walk rather than drive for short journeys, particularly the school run, and rightly so. However, parents should be able to walk their children to school without feeling that they are putting them at risk from passing traffic. This is a short journey that should be perfectly manageable on foot, but the condition of this pavement, combined with the speed and proximity of passing vehicles, makes it unnecessarily dangerous.

text: Risk To Traffic and Residents - Borders Overgrown Heights and Widths on Megstone Close Seahouses NE68 7XJ: Location Details: Properties Affected - The full street at Megstone Close Seahouses NE68 7XJ Owner of the queried land is - Hilltop & Stone Close Caravan Park on Mitchell Avenue, Seahouses. On the border between the Caravan Park and Megstone Close - this affects the residents down the full length of the private street. This should be cut down around twice a year, before summer and at the end of summer so the residents are not affected by this. We think this just an oversight but waited to see and it certainly hasn't been cut down in the past 5 years. Town/Village: Seahouses Description of the Issue: I am writing to report a severe, high-priority safety hazard regarding a parcel of land owned by the nearby caravan park at Hilltop & Stone Close on Mitchell Avenue. The vegetation on Megstone Close land has grown completely out of control, standing over 10 feet high and heavily encroaching onto the public road. This issue requires urgent enforcement intervention based on three distinct council policies and legal frameworks: 1. Highways Act 1980 (Immediate Road Obstruction): The overgrowth is spilling directly onto the road surface, forcing vehicles into the centre of the road and severely restricting visibility for drivers and pedestrians. 2. Severe Night-Time Safety Hazard (Loss of Light): Due to its 10-foot height, this wall of vegetation completely blocks out the street lighting on this section of the road. At night, it casts a massive shadow, making the street pitch black and entirely unsafe for pedestrians, elderly residents, and local traffic. It creates a major blind spot where oncoming vehicles cannot see people walking on the roadside or on bikes. Generally unsafe at night time. 3. Anti-social Behaviour Act 2003 / Part 8 (High Hedges Policy): The sheer height and density of this overgrown barrier is acting as a "high hedge" that is severely impacting the entire street. It is drastically blocking natural daylight and views from the front of neighbouring domestic properties. While the caravan park must cut the face of the vegetation vertically back to their boundary line, we request that Northumberland Council Highways and Environmental Health teams enforce a mandatory reduction in the total height of this overgrowth. It needs to be reduced to a safe level (such as 2 metres/6 feet) to restore critical road visibility, allow street lighting to illuminate the road safely at night, and return natural light to the affected residents. The caravan park has a good reputation and I am sure this is an oversight on their part. Please provide a ticket reference number and log this as an urgent safety investigation and could the Caravan park be told to maintain this as part of their yearly work. Kind regards, Megstone Close Residents

text: Sundown, Kingsthorpe, Alanby: Subject: Sea Lane, Huttoft – risk of further deterioration and request for preventative action before winter Dear Lincolnshire County Council Highways, I am increasingly concerned that the Council’s decision to continue monitoring the damaged section of Sea Lane, Huttoft, without providing a repair date could allow the condition of the road to deteriorate further. Sea Lane normally carries light traffic. However, during the Roman Bank/Huttoft Bank construction works, it was used for weeks by fully loaded LGV Class 2 construction vehicles. I personally counted one convoy of ten trucks within ten minutes, with trucks queuing at the junction with Roman Bank. The Council’s own report records a defect approximately 40 metres long, with an approximately 80 mm change in level. Sea Lane has no conventional drainage system, relying instead on water soaking away. I am concerned that rainwater entering the long tear could weaken the road structure and that freezing conditions over the coming winter could accelerate the deterioration, potentially turning a repairable defect into a much more extensive and costly failure. This concern must be considered alongside the assurance recorded in Huttoft Parish Council minutes that damage caused by construction traffic would be repaired under the contractor’s contractual obligations. Please confirm: 1. Whether the Council has assessed the risk of water ingress and further structural deterioration at this location. 2. Whether temporary sealing or other preventative work is required before freezing conditions occur. 3. Whether the contractor has been instructed to undertake the promised repairs. 4. Why the defect remains under monitoring despite the Council’s own recorded measurements. 5. The date of the next inspection and the criteria that will trigger remedial action. 6. Whether the Council has considered the potential additional cost of allowing the damage to deteriorate rather than undertaking preventative repairs now.

The location is marked with 2.0 m (6 ft 6 in) width-restriction signs and priority signs for oncoming traffic. The usable carriageway width appears to leave extremely limited clearance for vehicles.
